primitives.name: Single-number evaluation metric and the F1 harmonic mean
primitives.verbatim_quote: Having a single-number evaluation metric speeds up your ability to make a decision when you are selecting among a large number of classifiers.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Precision = fraction of predicted-positive examples that are truly positive, dimensionless ratio in (0,1], unit [1]; Recall = fraction of actual-positive examples correctly labeled, dimensionless ratio in (0,1], unit [1] (definitions printed in footnote 3, PDF p.20); F1 = harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, dimensionless in [0,1], unit [1]; the constant 2 and the arithmetic operators are dimensionless. The formula is printed verbatim in footnote 4 (PDF p.21) as 2/((1/Precision)+(1/Recall)). All terms are probability-like ratios, so the expression is dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.20-21): Precision and Recall trade off against each other (footnote 3); a single number gives a clear preference ranking among classifiers; averaging or weighted averaging is the common way to combine multiple metrics; F1 'works better than simply taking the mean'. The metric is computed on the dev (or test) set.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularities: F1 is undefined when Precision=0 or Recall=0 (division by zero in 1/Precision or 1/Recall); F1 tends to 0 as either tends to 0, so the harmonic mean is veto-sensitive — the weaker quantity dominates. A single number can also hide what matters: Chapter 11 (PDF p.26) gives the case where the more accurate classifier lets occasional pornographic images through, proving the metric itself must be changed when it measures something other than what the project needs.
timescales: tau_2 = per-iteration dev-set evaluation (hours to days)
tau_3 = metric redefinition when product needs change (project-scale)

layer2.mapping: The single-number metric is a scalarization kernel on a multi-objective decision space: it collapses a vector of criteria into a ranking so the team can iterate. In the 22-player football dynamical system this binds to the choice of a single optimizing objective (e.g., line-free expected points) over a vector of competing desiderata, with the harmonic-mean algebra supplying the veto shape: a near-zero recall on the tail class collapses the score regardless of precision elsewhere.
layer2.telemetry: Dev-set metric deltas between candidate models (the book's 0.1% detection example requires ~10,000 dev examples, PDF p.19); per-class precision and recall so the scalarization never hides a tail-class collapse; metric-vs-product-judgment disagreement as the trigger to redefine the metric.

primitives.name: Optimizing and satisficing metrics (constrained scalarization)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Then, maximize accuracy, subject to your classifier meeting the running time criteria.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.22-23): with N criteria, set N-1 as satisficing (must meet a threshold) and one as optimizing; example thresholds are running time at most 100ms and, for wakeword detection, no more than one false positive every 24 hours of operation while minimizing false negative rate. The book explicitly rejects the linear scalarization 'Accuracy - 0.5*RunningTime' as unnatural (PDF p.22).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The rejected formula Accuracy - 0.5*RunningTime is dimensionally inhomogeneous — a dimensionless probability minus a time in milliseconds — which is the deep reason it is 'unnatural': no choice of the coefficient 0.5 makes the subtraction unit-consistent without an implicit exchange rate. Satisficing thresholds can also silently exclude the best system if set wrong, and the book gives no procedure for choosing them beyond judgment. The constraint structure fails when the satisficing metric is itself noisy near the threshold.

layer2.mapping: Optimizing-under-satisficing-constraints is exactly the GSE veto architecture: expected value is the optimizing metric, while physiological, clinical, and roster constraints are satisficing metrics that must be met before any EV comparison is admissible. The wakeword false-positive budget is isomorphic to a hard exposure cap (challenge budget, DFS portfolio concentration limit): one optimizing objective under N-1 hard constraints, never a weighted sum that lets a high score buy its way past a constraint.
layer2.telemetry: Constraint-violation rate per candidate; the constrained optimum's optimizing-metric value; threshold sensitivity analysis (how the ranking changes as the satisficing bound moves); inference latency and false-positive counts per 24 h in the source setting.

primitives.name: Bias/variance error decomposition against the optimal (Bayes) error rate
primitives.verbatim_quote: There are two major sources of error in machine learning: bias and variance.
primitives.latex: \text{Bias} = \text{Optimal error rate (unavoidable bias)} + \text{Avoidable bias};\quad \text{Avoidable bias} = \text{Training error} - \text{Optimal error rate};\quad \text{Variance} = \text{Dev error} - \text{Training error}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Training error, Dev error = misclassification fractions on the respective sets, dimensionless probabilities in [0,1], unit [1 = one example]; Optimal error rate = Bayes error rate (named on PDF p.47), the infimum of achievable error, dimensionless in [0,1]; Avoidable bias = Training error minus Optimal error rate, dimensionless, normally >=0 (footnote 8, PDF p.47: a negative value means the algorithm has over-memorized the training set); Variance = Dev error minus Training error, dimensionless, normally >=0; Bias = sum of unavoidable and avoidable parts, dimensionless. Every term is an error probability, so all three identities are dimensionally homogeneous (probability = probability + probability). The printed line on PDF p.47 wraps 'unavoidable bias' in quotation marks as a label; the transcription drops only the quotation marks. Footnote 6 (PDF p.43) states Total Error = Bias + Variance is provable when the error metric is mean squared error — that identity is NOT asserted for 0-1 classification error.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.42-47): training, dev and test sets come from the same distribution (stated at the start of Chapter 20); the definitions are deliberately informal — footnotes 6 and 9 explicitly distinguish them from the statistical definitions of estimator bias and variance; human-level performance (ideally a team of experts, PDF p.68) serves as the proxy for the optimal error rate on tasks humans do well.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Negative avoidable bias signals over-memorization and redirects effort to variance reduction (footnote 8). When train and dev/test distributions differ, the two-term decomposition is insufficient and a data-mismatch term plus a Training-dev set are required (Chapters 40-41). The MSE identity Total Error = Bias + Variance does not transfer to classification error. On tasks humans cannot do (stock prediction, recommendation), the optimal error rate is hard to estimate and the whole diagnostic loses its anchor (PDF pp.48, 67).
timescales: tau_3 = learning-curve sweeps across training-set sizes (Chapter 28)

layer2.mapping: In the 22-player football dynamical system the decomposition separates three failure sources: unavoidable bias is the irreducible stochasticity of match outcomes (the Bayes error of football — even perfect information leaves randomness, which is why outputs must be distributions, never certainties); avoidable bias is model misspecification of the transition kernel; variance is overfitting to a small sample of matches; data mismatch is regime shift between training seasons and the target season. The Bayes floor is the invariant that vetoes any claim of deterministic prediction.
layer2.telemetry: Training error, Training-dev error, dev error measured on the four-set layout; learning curves (dev and training error vs training-set size) to test whether more data can help; expert-panel baseline as the Bayes-rate proxy; sign check on avoidable bias as the over-memorization alarm.

primitives.name: Optimization Verification test: separating search failure from scoring-function failure
primitives.verbatim_quote: Each dev example for which this inequality holds will get marked as an error caused by the optimization algorithm.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: A = input audio clip (data object, no physical unit); S = candidate output sentence (discrete string); S* = correct transcription, S_out = system's actual output (discrete strings); Score_A(S) = P(S|A) = conditional probability that S is the correct transcription given audio A, dimensionless probability measure in [0,1], unit [1]; the inequality compares two probabilities and is dimensionally homogeneous. The general form (PDF p.87) replaces A with any input x and S with any response y: Score_x(y). The reinforcement-learning variant (PDF pp.88-89) uses Score(T) = R(T), a hand-designed dimensionless reward scalar over trajectories T (the book's example assigns R(T) = -1,000 for a crash); T_human and T_out are the human-pilot and algorithm trajectories. Beam search keeps K top candidates (K a dimensionless integer count).
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.85-89): the scoring function can be evaluated on any candidate output, including the known-correct one; the search is approximate (beam search is not guaranteed to find the arg max); the correct output y* is available from dev labels, or a superior reference output exists (T_human in the RL case, assumed good but not optimal); the pattern is 'first learn an approximate scoring function, then use an approximate maximization algorithm'.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The test cannot run if Score is intractable to evaluate on arbitrary candidates, or if no correct/superior reference output exists. Attribution is per-example: the aggregate fraction (the book's 95% scoring / 5% search example) is a ceiling on what improving the other component can achieve. In the RL variant the comparison is to human-level rather than optimal output, so the conclusion is directional, not definitive. The test diagnoses attribution, not magnitude: a component blamed for 5% of errors may still be cheap to fix.
timescales: tau_1 = per-decision scoring and search (inference time)

layer2.mapping: This is the GSE failure-attribution invariant: when a high-EV call fails, re-score the known-superior action under the value model. If the model ranks the superior action above the chosen one, the failure is in search/execution (play selection, clock management, the coach's decision procedure); if the model ranks the inferior action higher, the failure is in the scoring function (the EV model itself). It binds to the belief-to-action transition of the 22-player system and prevents the classic error of retraining the value model when the optimizer was at fault, or vice versa.
layer2.telemetry: Per-decision logs of Score(chosen) vs Score(reference-superior); the fraction of dev-set failures attributed to search vs objective; beam-width sensitivity in the source setting; in GSE, replay re-scoring of the best alternative call under the frozen pre-decision model.

primitives.name: Error-analysis ceiling and the Eyeball/Blackbox dev split
primitives.verbatim_quote: You will more rapidly overfit the portion that you are manually looking at.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.30-31, 36-38): manually examine ~100 misclassified dev examples and count error categories; the category fraction is a ceiling on the error reduction any fix for that category can deliver (5% dog errors caps the dog-fix at 5% of errors, i.e. 90% to at best 90.5% accuracy); the Eyeball dev set is randomly selected and manually examined, the Blackbox dev set is used only for automatic evaluation; divergence between Eyeball and Blackbox performance detects manual overfitting; ~100 errors gives a very good sense of error sources, ~10 is very small (PDF p.38).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Categories overlap, so percentages need not sum to 100% (PDF p.32). The ceiling assumes a fix could eliminate the entire category, which is an upper bound rarely attained. Small error counts give noisy category fractions. On tasks humans cannot do well, Eyeball analysis loses its power because humans cannot explain the errors (PDF p.38). Fixing only misclassified labels introduces evaluation bias (PDF p.35).
timescales: tau_2 = ~2 hours of manual analysis per 100 examples (the book's estimate, PDF p.31)
tau_3 = Eyeball-set refresh when overfitting is detected

layer2.mapping: The ceiling calculation is an intervention-EV upper bound for the 22-player system: before investing in any fix (a new press trigger, a coverage adjustment, a feature), count the fraction of observed failures it could possibly address — that fraction caps its value. The Eyeball/Blackbox split binds to the separation between manual film study (which overfits the analyst's intuition) and held-out game outcomes (which stay unbiased): GSE must keep a Blackbox evaluation lane that no analyst eyeballs during development.
layer2.telemetry: Error-category counts on ~100 sampled failures; Eyeball-vs-Blackbox performance divergence as the manual-overfitting alarm; category overlap matrix; post-fix realized error reduction vs the pre-computed ceiling.

primitives.name: Four-set diagnostic: bias, variance, and data mismatch under distribution shift
primitives.verbatim_quote: This algorithm suffers from high avoidable bias and from data mismatch.
primitives.assumptions: As printed (PDF pp.77-80): four subsets — Training set (may mix distributions), Training-dev set (same distribution as training, never trained on), Dev set and Test set (both from the target distribution the system must do well on); comparing training error, training-dev error, and dev error separates high avoidable bias, high variance, and data mismatch; the worked example is 10% training / 11% training-dev / 20% dev error = high avoidable bias plus data mismatch, not high variance. Chapter 36 adds the governing rule: choose dev and test sets to reflect data you expect to get in the future and want to do well on.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Requires enough labeled data to staff four sets. If the target distribution is nonstationary, even the dev set is only a proxy for the future, and the book's own footnote 11 (PDF p.71) warns that under large distribution shift luck — including hand-designed features — dominates outcomes, making systematic study difficult. The diagnostic cannot detect mismatch between the dev set and the true future distribution; that requires the judgment call of Chapter 5.
timescales: tau_3 = season-scale distribution shift (the football binding)

layer2.mapping: Direct isomorphism to GSE's temporal generalization problem: training on past seasons (distribution A) while predicting future seasons (distribution B). Training-dev = held-out matches from the training seasons; dev/test = the most recent matches; the data-mismatch term is exactly regime shift (rule changes, coaching turnover, player movement). The four-set layout is the diagnostic that tells GSE whether a failing model needs more capacity (bias), more data (variance), or distribution-matching work (mismatch) — three different queues that a single train/test gap conflates.
layer2.telemetry: The four error rates (training, training-dev, dev, test); per-season error drift; subset performance on target-distribution examples embedded in training (the book's car-noise validation trick, PDF p.81); mismatch confirmed when training-distribution generalization is good but target-distribution error is high.

reasoning_traces.think: The deepest invariant in this book is that an evaluation metric is a decision procedure, not a measurement. Ng's cat-startup frame makes the stakes explicit: a team under pressure has dozens of plausible directions — more data, bigger network, smaller network, regularization, architecture changes — and choosing poorly wastes months. The single-number metric exists to make that choice fast and rankable. But the book immediately shows the metric's failure mode: precision and recall give two numbers and no ranking, so they must be combined; the harmonic mean F1 = 2/((1/Precision)+(1/Recall)) is chosen over the arithmetic mean because it is veto-sensitive — a classifier that misses most of the positive class cannot buy a high score with precision alone. That algebraic shape is the book's first cross-layer veto in miniature: the binding constraint dominates the favorable one. The second failure mode is subtler and appears in Chapter 11: the more accurate classifier lets occasional pornographic images through, and suddenly the metric itself is wrong. The lesson is that a metric is a proxy for product value, and when proxy and value diverge, the proxy must be replaced, not defended. This is exactly the discipline GSE needs when a headline accuracy number diverges from decision value: the number is a quoted claim under audit, never a win-rate headline. The optimizing/satisficing structure is the book's cleanest architectural contribution. The rejected formula Accuracy - 0.5*RunningTime is not merely 'unnatural' — it is dimensionally inhomogeneous, subtracting milliseconds from a probability. No coefficient repairs a unit mismatch without an implicit, unstable exchange rate. The correct structure is constrained optimization: maximize accuracy subject to running time at most 100ms; minimize wakeword false negatives subject to at most one false positive per 24 hours. N-1 constraints, one objective. This is isomorphic to the GSE veto stack: expected value is the optimizing metric, and physiological, clinical, and roster constraints are satisficing metrics that no EV score may override. A 95%-accurate classifier at 1500ms is vetoed by the 100ms constraint exactly as a high-EV deep-pass script is vetoed by a quarterback's shoulder limitation. The constraint layer sits below the decision layer, and the book's own example proves the ordering matters. The bias/variance decomposition adds the third invariant: error has sources, and the sources dictate the remedy. High avoidable bias calls for a bigger model or better features; high variance calls for more data or regularization; adding data to a high-bias model is wasted effort. The optimal error rate — the Bayes rate — anchors the whole diagnostic. On tasks humans do well, an expert panel's error is an upper bound on the Bayes rate, and the gap between training error and that bound is the avoidable bias. The book's footnotes are scrupulously honest that these are informal definitions, not the statistical bias and variance of estimators, and that Total Error = Bias + Variance is provable only for mean squared error. That honesty is itself a sovereign lesson: know which regime your identity holds in. For football, the Bayes floor is the irreducible stochasticity of 22-player outcomes — even perfect information leaves randomness — so any system claiming deterministic prediction has violated the decomposition at its root. Finally, the Eyeball/Blackbox split names a scar every analyst carries: the portion of data you manually study overfits your intuition faster than the portion you only score automatically. The divergence between the two is the alarm. GSE's film-study lane is an Eyeball set; the held-out outcome lane must remain Blackbox, or the foundry will optimize its own intuition and call it progress.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The book's own genealogy runs from the data-scarce era, when a random 70%/30% split was the common rule because only one dataset existed (Chapters 5 and 36), to the big-data era where dev/test fractions shrink while absolute sizes grow. The bias/variance vocabulary descends from statistics, and Ng's footnotes 6 and 9 explicitly mark where his informal usage departs from the formal definitions — a lineage acknowledged, not fabricated. The capacity metaphor is borrowed, with citation, from Sherlock Holmes in A Study in Scarlet: the brain as a finite attic where useless facts elbow out useful ones. The historical scar shaping the book is teams wasting months on directions that error analysis would have vetoed in two hours.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Model the team recursively. The enthusiastic engineer proposes a month-long dog-detector fix, anticipating the lead will approve because the idea is exciting; the lead, modeling that enthusiasm, demands the ceiling count first — what fraction of errors are dogs? — because the lead models the engineer's incentive to implement rather than measure. The engineer, modeling the lead's skepticism, learns to pitch evidence instead of excitement. In the GSE transfer the same recursion runs between coach, coordinator, and quarterback: the coach's comfort call anticipates the defense's look; the defensive coordinator sets a tendency trap keyed to that comfort; the quarterback's internal clock overrides both when his body knows the deep progression is unavailable. Each mind models the next, and the metric — or the veto — is the only object outside the recursion that can break the loop.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The satisficing constraint vetoes the optimizing metric: the 95%-accurate classifier at 1500ms is inadmissible under the 100ms bound regardless of its accuracy advantage, because the constraint layer is below the decision layer and no weighted sum may trade across it. The dimensional veto is the same shape: Accuracy - 0.5*RunningTime is rejected because probability minus time is not a quantity. In GSE, physiology vetoes EV — a congested-recovery squad or a limited quarterback forbids the script the value model prefers — and the Bayes floor vetoes any intervention claiming to beat irreducible error. The favorable layer proposes; the binding layer disposes.

reasoning_traces.think: The second cluster of invariants is about attribution before intervention. The Optimization Verification test is the book's most transferable diagnostic: a system that learns an approximate scoring function Score_x(y) and then approximately maximizes it can fail in exactly two places — the search or the score. When the speech system outputs 'I love robots' instead of 'I love machine learning', the test computes Score_A(S*) and Score_A(S_out) and asks which is larger. If the correct sentence scores higher, the scoring function did its job and the search failed; if not, the scoring function is at fault. The aggregate fraction is a ceiling: if 95% of errors are scoring errors, no amount of search improvement eliminates more than 5%. The reinforcement-learning variant replaces the correct output with a superior human trajectory — the helicopter autorotation example — and the same inequality R(T_human) > R(T_out) separates reward-design failure from policy-optimization failure. This is precisely the GSE failure-attribution problem. When a high-EV call fails, the foundry must re-score the known-superior alternative under the frozen pre-decision model. If the model ranked the better call higher, the failure is in selection or execution — the coach's decision procedure, clock management, the play-caller's search. If the model ranked the worse call higher, the failure is in the value function. Retraining the value model when the optimizer was at fault is the exact waste the test prevents, and the reverse error is equally costly. Error analysis by parts generalizes the test to pipelines: replace component A's output with a perfect hand-labeled output and rerun the rest; if the system now succeeds, blame A; otherwise move downstream. The DAG ordering requirement is the hidden assumption — attribution is only valid when later components depend solely on earlier outputs, and swapping independent components changes the fractions slightly but not the validity. The flawed-pipeline chapter adds the deepest structural veto: if every component is at human-level performance given its inputs, but the whole system is far below human-level, the pipeline itself is flawed — the inputs do not contain enough information. The self-driving example needs lane markings; no improvement to car detection, pedestrian detection, or path planning can recover information the pipeline discarded. For GSE this is the warning that a Coach-Mind sim can have every module calibrated and still fail because a state variable — fatigue, weather, travel, circadian load — was never wired into the pipeline at all. The four-set diagnostic completes the attribution toolkit under distribution shift. Training error, training-dev error, and dev error separate avoidable bias, variance, and data mismatch; the worked example of 10%/11%/20% shows bias plus mismatch without variance. This is the exact structure of GSE's temporal problem: train on past seasons, predict future seasons, and the data-mismatch term is regime shift. The book's governing rule — dev and test sets must reflect the data you expect to get in the future — is the same invariant as held-out discipline, and its footnote 11 honesty about luck dominating under large shifts is the reason GSE treats season-boundary generalization as a first-class risk rather than an afterthought. Across all these tools the meta-lesson is identical: measure the ceiling, attribute the error, and only then intervene. Two hours of counting saves a month of building, and one re-scoring inequality saves a quarter of misdirected retraining.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The scoring-function-plus-approximate-search pattern is the classical AI design pattern the book names explicitly (Chapter 45), descending from speech recognition's Score_A(S) = P(S|A) formulation and from reinforcement learning's hand-designed reward functions — the helicopter autorotation example is Ng's own research lineage, described in the text without invented dates. The pipeline-attribution method descends from the modular computer-vision and speech pipelines (MFCC features, phonemes) that end-to-end learning later challenged. The historical scar is teams randomly choosing to improve search or score without knowing which was at fault, and pipelines that discarded information no downstream component could recover.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Recursive belief clash under pressure: the offensive coordinator calls the tendency play because he believes the defense expects the comfort call; the defensive coordinator, modeling that belief, shows the comfort look pre-snap and rotates into the trap post-snap; the quarterback, modeling both, checks to the hot read because his internal clock knows the protection will not hold for the deep progression. Each layer models the next, and the pipeline's information set determines who can see the trap. The GSE sim must model this recursion explicitly — a value function that ignores the defense's model of the offense's model prices the trap as a normal coverage. The Optimization Verification test then asks, after the failed play, whether the model saw the trap and the caller ignored it, or the model never saw it at all.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The information-set veto is binding: if every pipeline component is at human-level given its inputs but the system is not, no component-level improvement is admissible as a fix — the pipeline must be redesigned to carry the missing state variable, because optimizing a module cannot recover discarded information. The data-mismatch veto is equally hard: a model with excellent training-distribution generalization but high target-distribution error cannot be promoted on its training metrics, however favorable; the mismatch must be addressed first. And the Bayes-floor veto from the decomposition forbids chasing training error below the irreducible rate — negative avoidable bias is over-memorization, not progress. Each veto sits below the EV calculation and overrides it.

universal_lens: The polymath lens this book trains is attribution-before-intervention: every improvement decision is a diagnosis problem, so measure the ceiling of a fix before investing, separate scoring-function failure from search failure with a single re-scoring inequality, and decompose error into irreducible, avoidable, and shift-induced parts before choosing a remedy. Keep the evaluation distribution aligned with the deployment distribution, keep a Blackbox lane that manual study cannot contaminate, and treat any metric that diverges from product value as a metric to be replaced. These habits transfer unchanged to physiology, finance, and any engineered system with a value function and a search procedure.
gsi_mapping: The Bayes error floor maps to irreducible physiological variability — no load model predicts injury or performance with zero error, and claims otherwise violate the decomposition. The Eyeball/Blackbox split maps to clinician chart review (which overfits the reviewer) versus automated telemetry scoring (which stays unbiased). Data mismatch maps to training a load or recovery model on one population or sport and deploying on another. Optimizing/satisficing maps directly to clinical practice: recovery time or performance is the optimizing metric, while concussion protocols, axonal shear risk thresholds, and cardiac limits are satisficing constraints that no performance gain may override.
gse_mapping: Optimizing-under-satisficing is the GSE veto stack: line-free expected value is the optimizing metric under hard physiological, clinical, and roster constraints. The bias/variance/data-mismatch decomposition separates model misspecification, small-sample overfitting, and season regime shift — three different queues a single train/test gap conflates. The Optimization Verification test attributes failed calls to play selection versus the EV model by re-scoring the superior alternative under the frozen pre-decision model. Eyeball/Blackbox separates film study from held-out outcomes. No sportsbook odds enter any layer; artifacts are internal and never published.
